name: Sam Wagner

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for sitting down with me. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to companies, unions or parties. Everything you say stays confidential. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I get into Brickyard Studio about nine. It's six of us above a bike shop on Canal Street. Most of my week is menus, gig posters and flyers for cafés and music venues in the old town. I still sketch everything in pencil, ink it and scan it, which Marta, my boss, calls slow but charming. The bit that wears me out is resizing the same poster into eleven social media sizes at five o'clock.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like most about it?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: When a band comes in and sees their poster on the wall for the first time. I'm not the best designer in the room, and Kofi, our senior designer, fixes my spacing most weeks. But my hand-drawn style is something clients ask for by name. Two years in, I'm still learning the grown-up parts, like pricing and pitching.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so, honestly. Everyone was posting about the end of design, and it turned out to be fancy autofill. I'd probably put up a hand-drawn poster that says still made by people and leave it at that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be relieved but not off the hook. Junior pay at Brickyard just about covers my half of the rent with Lena, and two of our café clients closed this year anyway. Even the boring version of AI eats the resizing and the menu updates, which is a chunk of what a junior gets paid for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly keep doing what I do and get faster at the parts I'm slow at. I'd keep putting about a hundred a month into savings so we stay near three months' rent. I might finally do the evening screen-printing course at the community print workshop, because I love it and nobody can autofill a squeegee.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly relief, like a storm that missed. But there's a low hum of worry that was there before anyone said AI, about whether a junior on my money ever gets to be a senior.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said two café clients closed. What happens at Brickyard if a couple more go?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Marta would cut hours before she cut people, she's said as much. So I'd probably drop to four days, and four days of my pay doesn't cover my half of the rent on Hollis Road. Lena would cover the gap for a while, but she's on care-home wages, so that isn't a real plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you talk to about that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Kofi first, because he's lived through two agencies closing. Then the illustrators' group chat I'm in, where we moan about late invoices. We talk a lot about forming a proper union for juniors and freelancers, but nobody's ever organised it.

I'd put up a **hand-drawn poster** saying the work is still made by people.
think: Junior pay only just covers **half the rent** he shares with Lena.
Even weak AI eats the **resizing** and menu updates that juniors are paid for.

Sign up for the evening **screen-printing course** at the community workshop.
feel: **Relief**, like a storm that missed him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is exactly what happens when nobody regulates these companies. They trained the image tools on work by people like me, and now they sell it back to my clients. I'd be loud about it online, and I'd say the government should make them pay for what they took.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be in trouble faster than most. I don't use the tools, I'm slow, and the junior jobs are the ones Marta could hand to software: the resizing, the first draft of a menu, the flyer text. Kofi would be fine, he's the one clients trust. I'm the one who costs a salary to do what the box does in a minute.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First I'd have an honest talk with Marta about what she expects from me in a year. I'd push the screen printing harder, two nights a week, and try to get Brickyard to sell printed posters so my job has a hands-on part. And I'd finally help set up that union for juniors and freelancers, even just a dozen of us with a shared rate card.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Angry, mostly, and a bit ashamed underneath it. Angry because it feels like theft, ashamed because I know I've been stubborn about learning anything new.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've said you never use the AI tools. Would that change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably a little, if Marta made it part of the job, but I'd drag my feet. Every time I've tried one, it gave me a poster that looked like every other poster. I'd rather get good at something the machine is bad at than become a worse version of the machine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If your hours were cut, what would you cut at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The car goes first. I only use it to see my mum in Westbrook once a month, and I can take the train. Then eating out, which hurts because half our clients are restaurants. Lena and I already talked about a cheaper flat when the lease is up in March.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't think I'd say much in public at first, I'd be too stunned. If anything I'd be at a march or posting about a jobs guarantee, because people like me can't sort this out alone. You can't adapt by yourself to something that does your whole job in two years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think the design part of my job is gone by 2028, and I'm one of the first out. The only part with any time left is the hands-on stuff, screen printing and sign painting, maybe three years until robots do that well. Three years of screen printing before the robots catch up is not a career, it's a waiting room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Right away I'd stop spending on anything but rent and food and try to grow our savings from three months to six. I'd go to the print workshop and ask Dagmar, who runs it, whether she'd take me on part-time, even for less money. And I'd join whatever union or campaign was fighting for income support, because I'd need it, and so would most of my friends.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick, honestly. Like the floor dropped and everybody's still pretending it's fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the print workshop. How long could that last you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If robots come around 2031, maybe until then, maybe a bit longer, because a small community workshop won't buy a robot in the first year. But Dagmar runs it on grants and course fees, and if everybody's broke, nobody pays for evening classes. So I'd be swapping one shaky thing for another.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Lena that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my girlfriend Lena she's probably safer than me for a while, because nobody's replacing a care worker in two years. That's a strange thing to say to your partner, that you might be living off her. She'd say we'll manage, and I'd half believe her.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got five years, so let's use them properly, which means rules, retraining money and a say for workers. I'd be pushing the union idea hard by then, not just talking about it in a group chat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years doesn't save my design job, it just means I watch it shrink instead of losing it overnight. By about 2029 I reckon Marta's down to Kofi and a laptop. The difference is I'd have time to get properly good at something hands-on before the robots arrive around 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'd start proper training in sign painting, evenings first, then drop to four days at Brickyard. I'd save harder, two hundred a month instead of one hundred, and Lena and I would skip the bigger flat we'd been eyeing. And I'd get the juniors' union actually registered, with dues and a lawyer, so we have something when the layoffs start.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Less sick than the fast one, more like dread with a to-do list. Five years feels long when you're twenty-seven and short when it's the only five years you get to change trades.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd move toward hands-on work, but the robots come in 2034. Why bother?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because three extra years matter when you're starting from nothing. A hand-painted shop sign might be something people still pay a person for even when a robot can do it, like people still buy hand-thrown mugs. I might be kidding myself, but it's the only part of my job that feels like mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at Brickyard would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Priya, our account manager, because so much of her job is emails, quotes and scheduling, and that goes first. Kofi will be fine for a few years, clients like him. Priya and I would be having the same nervous lunch.

I'd push the **union** for real instead of only in a group chat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With ten years, I'd say this is a political choice, not a natural disaster. There's time to set up retraining and income support, so if it goes badly, it's because the people in charge chose not to bother.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years is actually enough to change trades properly, which is a strange relief. I'd be thirty-seven when the design work goes and about forty when the robots catch up. I still think junior design jobs disappear, but I'd have a decade to stop being a junior at something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, in the first year I'd probably do less than I should, because ten years feels far away and I hate change. I'd keep the screen-printing course going and keep saving. The bigger step would be talking to Dagmar about buying into the print workshop as a co-op member over a few years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calmer, but suspicious of my own calm. I know myself, I'll use the time to put things off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd do less than you should. What would push you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Seeing Kofi lose work, probably. If the guy who fixes my spacing is struggling, then I know it's real. Or Lena sitting me down with a spreadsheet, which she's done before about the car.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still want to be a designer in ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want to be someone who makes things with his hands that people put on their walls. Whether that's called graphic design or printmaking doesn't matter much to me. What I don't want is to type prompts for a living.

With ten years, a bad outcome means leaders **chose not to** prepare people.

Junior design work still disappears, but I'd have a **decade** to grow.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, easily, because there's no time to learn a new trade and my savings last about three months. What would help is income support that doesn't make you grovel, and paid training in hands-on trades, like a year's wage while you apprentice at a print shop. If I'm honest, a kick to start learning now would help too.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask who owns the tools. Brickyard doesn't, Marta doesn't, I don't. It's a few huge companies, and that's the part nobody voted for. If designers ended up as the people who own a share of the machine, I'd feel completely different about all of this.

headlineQuote: If designers ended up as the people who own a share of the machine, I'd feel completely different about all of this.
portrait: Sam is a **27-year-old junior designer** at Brickyard, a six-person agency making menus and gig posters.
He draws by hand, **never uses AI tools**, and shares rent with Lena, a care worker.
His **left-leaning politics** shape every answer: regulation, unions and income support come first.
He plans an escape into **screen printing**, knowing robots only buy him about three years.
With ten years' warning he feels calmer but expects to **put things off**.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because there's no time to learn a new trade.
His savings would last only about **three months**.
whatWouldHelp: Income support **without groveling** and paid apprenticeships in hands-on trades.
A **kick** to start learning now, and designers owning a **share** of AI.
